newsitem.title: UK: UK talks tough on rights in Bosnia, Indonesia.
newsitem.headline: UK talks tough on rights in Bosnia, Indonesia.

text.p: Foreign Secretary Robin Cook promised a new crackdown on Thursday against Bosnia's war criminals as part of his pledge to put human rights at the heart of British foreign policy.
He also said there would be new restrictions on the export of arms to nations such as Indonesia, which human rights groups accuse of using British weapons for internal repression.
"There will be changes with respect to a number of countries, of which that is one," he told BBC radio.
Britain's new Labour government has promised to make human rights an integral part of foreign policy and Cook was due to put flesh on the bones of that pledge in a speech later on Thursday.
On the former Yugoslavia, Cook said there was no prospect of true reconciliation so long as those who committed atrocities during the 1992-95 Bosnian war remained at large.

A week ago, British troops in the NATO-led Stabilisation Force in Bosnia shot dead Simo Drljaca, former police chief in the town of Prijedor, when he resisted arrest. They also seized the director of Prijedor hospital and extradited him to face trial in The Hague. Both had been indicted for warcrimes.

"Justice is an important pre-condition of reconciliation in Bosnia. These people flouted international law. As a member of the international community, we must not leave any hiding place in the world for those who break the world's rules," Cook told BBC television.
He promised to announce an "important commitment" to the war crimes tribunal in The Hague that should speed up trials.
Critics say his rights crusade could hurt British exports and make little difference on a world stage where Britain is no longer a top player.

But Cook said: "Of course Britain cannot do it alone. I'm not pretending that we are going to create a perfect world. We can make a very serious improvement. We can make a difference. As a result of our works, some improvements will take place in some countries, some regimes may be fearful about using the worst excesses of violence and some dissidents will go free."
Cook dismissed suggestions that Britain should sever trading links with nations that violate human rights, saying maintaining contact would have more influence.

But he said some countries, such as Iraq, were beyond constructive dialogue. As for Nigeria, he said Britain would recommend its continued exclusion from the Commonwealth unless there was a big improvement in human rights.
